nameStory: The Red Cushion Star gets its name from its distinctive puffy, pillow-like appearance and vibrant red coloration. The word 'cushion' perfectly captures how this starfish looks like a soft, rounded cushion sitting on the ocean floor. Even its scientific name 'pulvillus' means 'little cushion' in Latin, showing that scientists were struck by the same cozy resemblance!
description: The Red Cushion Star is a charming marine animal that belongs to the starfish family, living on the ocean floor along New England's coast. Unlike the classic flat, pointy-armed starfish most people picture, this species has a thick, rounded body with short, stubby arms that blend smoothly into its central disk. It typically grows to about 2-4 inches across and has a distinctly puffy, inflated appearance. Its bright red to orange-red color makes it stand out beautifully against the sandy or rocky sea bottom.

idTips.label: Cushion-like shape
idTips.description: The body is noticeably thick and puffy like a small pillow, with arms that are barely distinguishable from the central disk - very different from typical flat starfish

idTips.label: Bright red color
idTips.description: Vibrant red to orange-red coloration that's consistent across the entire body surface, making it easily spotted underwater

idTips.label: Smooth texture
idTips.description: The surface feels relatively smooth to the touch with small, barely noticeable bumps, unlike the rough or spiny texture of many other starfish species

idTips.label: Short, blunt arms
idTips.description: Five arms that are very short and rounded, appearing more like lobes than the distinct pointed arms of other starfish

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Compact size that fits easily in the palm of your hand, rarely exceeding 4 inches across

habitat: Red Cushion Stars inhabit the rocky subtidal zones and deeper waters along New England's coast, typically found at depths ranging from 30 feet to several hundred feet below the surface. They prefer areas with hard rocky substrates, often hiding in crevices or under ledges where they can find shelter. You're most likely to encounter them while scuba diving or snorkeling in deeper coastal waters, particularly around rocky reefs and boulder fields.

seasonality.spring: Active feeding season as water temperatures begin to warm, though they remain in deeper waters beyond typical shore exploration.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when divers are most likely to spot them moving slowly across rocky surfaces or nestled in crevices during daylight hours.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may begin moving to slightly deeper waters as surface temperatures start to cool.
seasonality.winter: Less active in the coldest months, often remaining hidden in rock crevices and moving very little.

funFact: Red Cushion Stars are living vacuum cleaners of the sea floor - they can actually push their stomach outside of their body to digest food externally, allowing them to eat prey much larger than their tiny mouth could normally accommodate!
confusionNotes: The Red Cushion Star is most commonly confused with other red starfish species, but its distinctive puffy, cushion-like shape makes it unique. Remember: if it looks like a red pillow with barely visible arms rather than a classic flat star shape, you've found a Red Cushion Star!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'starfish,' Red Cushion Stars are not fish at all - they're echinoderms, more closely related to sea urchins and sand dollars. The preferred scientific term is 'sea star' to avoid this confusion, though both names are widely understood.
compareHints: Since the Red Cushion Star is the only Porania species found in New England waters, compare it to other small red sea stars in the region. Unlike the common Northern Sea Star which has long, distinct arms and a flat profile, the Red Cushion Star's arms are so short and rounded they barely extend from the central body. Other red starfish in New England waters tend to be either much larger or have the classic flat, pointed-arm appearance that the Red Cushion Star distinctly lacks.
